title: Fibre-component generic points are relative associated points
statement: Let $f:X\to S$ be a flat morphism of schemes locally of finite type [def-weil-flat-morphism, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. For $t\in S$, let $X_t$ be the scheme-theoretic fibre [def-pc-scheme-fibre], and let $y$ be the generic point [def-sc-generic-point] of an irreducible component [def-weil-irreducible-components] of $X_t$. Then $y$ is an associated point of the fibre structure sheaf $\mathcal O_{X_t}$ [def-sc-associated-points], hence belongs to the relative assassin $\operatorname{Ass}_{X/S}(\mathcal O_X)$, defined as the union over $s\in S$ of the associated points of $\mathcal O_{X_s}$.

proof.text: Put $T=X_t$ and $K=\kappa(t)$. By the fibre definition, $T\to\operatorname{Spec}K$ is the base change of $f$ along $\operatorname{Spec}K\to S$. The locally-finite-type base-change lemma therefore makes this morphism locally of finite type. A field has only the ideals $(0)$ and $(1)$, both finitely generated, so $K$ is Noetherian and its one-point spectrum is locally Noetherian. Applying the locally-Noetherian finite-type lemma gives that $T$ is locally Noetherian. Neither this argument nor the remaining steps require any Noetherian hypothesis on $S$.

Let $B$ be the component of $T$ with generic point $y$. Choose from the locally Noetherian affine cover an affine neighbourhood $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $y$ with $A$ Noetherian, and let $\mathfrak p\subset A$ be its prime corresponding to $y$ under the affine-open point identification. We check directly that $\mathfrak p$ is minimal. In the Zariski topology $\overline{\{\mathfrak p\}}=V(\mathfrak p)$: a closed set $V(I)$ contains $\mathfrak p$ exactly when $I\subseteq\mathfrak p$, so every such closed set contains $V(\mathfrak p)$. Also $B\cap U=\overline{\{y\}}^{\,U}=V(\mathfrak p)$; the equality of closures follows because $U$ is an open neighbourhood of $y$. If a prime $\mathfrak q\subsetneq\mathfrak p$ existed, its point $z\in U$ would specialize to $y$, since $\mathfrak p\in V(\mathfrak q)$. Thus the closure of $z$ in $T$ contains $B$. That closure is irreducible (a singleton is irreducible, and its closure remains irreducible directly by the closed-set definition), so maximality of the component $B$ makes it equal to $B$. But $z\notin B\cap U=V(\mathfrak p)$ because $\mathfrak p\nsubseteq\mathfrak q$, a contradiction. This proves minimality without assuming $T$ irreducible or reduced.

proof.text: Apply the Noetherian minimal-prime associated-prime lemma to $A$ and $\mathfrak p$. Step 1 and the choice in Step 2 give precisely its Noetherian hypothesis; Step 2 gives its minimal-prime hypothesis. It supplies $a\in A$ with $\operatorname{Ann}_A(a)=\mathfrak p$. Thus $\mathfrak p$ is an associated prime of $A$.

The associated-prime localization lemma, applied to this Noetherian ring $A$ and its associated prime $\mathfrak p$, says that the maximal ideal $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$ is associated to $A_{\mathfrak p}$. By the affine-open stalk-localization theorem, the germ map identifies $\mathcal O_{T,y}$ with $A_{\mathfrak p}$. Under this ring isomorphism maximal ideals correspond, and an annihilator equality corresponds because $rb=0$ is preserved and reflected by a ring isomorphism. Consequently the maximal ideal of $\mathcal O_{T,y}$ is the annihilator of an element of that ring. By the definition of associated points, $y\in\operatorname{Ass}_T(\mathcal O_T)$.

proof.text: In the union defining $\operatorname{Ass}_{X/S}(\mathcal O_X)$ in the statement, take the index $s=t$. The preceding step places $y$ in its summand $\operatorname{Ass}_{X_t}(\mathcal O_{X_t})$. Regard this point as a point of $X$ by the fibre projection, whose underlying map identifies $X_t$ with $f^{-1}(t)$. Thus $y\in\operatorname{Ass}_{X/S}(\mathcal O_X)$, as required.
